title: Booleans and if
summary: Ask yes-or-no questions about your data, and run different code depending on the answer.

steps.title: Questions with a yes or no answer
body: So far every program ran the same statements every time. To make a decision, a program first has to ask a question.
A **comparison** is a question. Its answer is a `bool`: `true` or `false`.
| `<=` `>=` | less than or equal? greater than or equal? |
> **Tip:** `=` stores a value. `==` compares two values. Mixing them up is the classic beginner bug.

steps.prompt: Match each operator to the question it asks.
pairs: is the left at least as big as the right?
is the left smaller than the right?
not a question: stores a value

steps.title: if, else if, else
body: `if` runs a block of code only when its condition is `true`.
The conditions are checked **from the top**. The first one that is true wins, and the rest are skipped. `else` has no condition: it catches everything that is left.
`else if` and `else` are optional. You can have as many `else if` parts as you need, but only one `else`, and it comes last.

steps.explain: `18 > 25` is false, so the first block is skipped. `18 > 15` is true, so `Mild` prints and the `else` is skipped. The last line is outside the `if`, so it always runs.

steps.prompt: Arrange the lines so a `score` of 90 or more prints `A`, 70 to 89 prints `B`, and anything lower prints `C`.
steps.explain: The strictest test goes first. If `score >= 70` came first, a score of 95 would stop there and print `B`. When a branch is a single statement the braces may be left out, as here.

steps.title: Fix the grader
prompt: This program reads a score and should print:
It has **two** mistakes. One stops it compiling. The other makes it give the wrong answer for high scores.
hints: `else` never takes a condition. It means "everything that is left".
Conditions are checked from the top and the first true one wins. What happens to a score of 95 at the first `if`?
Test `score >= 80` first, then `score >= 50`, and finish with a plain `else`.

steps.title: Combining conditions
body: Real questions often have two parts: *is the user logged in **and** an admin?* Three **logical operators** join or flip bools.
- `a && b` means **and**: true when both are true.
- `a || b` means **or**: true when at least one is true.
To test a range, write both comparisons: `age >= 13 && age <= 19`. The maths shorthand `13 <= age <= 19` does not compile in C#.
> **Tip:** `&&` is worked out before `||`. When you mix them, add parentheses so nobody has to remember that.

steps.prompt: Given `int age = 20;` and `bool member = false;`, is each expression true or false?
A ride is open to you when you are **at least** 120 cm tall **and** you have a ticket. Complete the condition.
steps.explain: "At least 120" includes 120 itself, so it is `>=` and not `>`. Both parts must hold, so they are joined with `&&`.

steps.title: The ternary operator
body: Often an `if`/`else` exists only to pick one of two values. The **ternary operator** does that in a single expression:
Read `?` as "then" and `:` as "otherwise". Use it for short choices between two values. For anything longer, or for running statements, an `if` is clearer.

steps.explain: `3 > 5` is false, so the ternary gives the value after the `:`. A ternary always produces exactly one of its two values.

steps.title: Leap year
prompt: Read a year and print `Leap year` or `Common year`.
A year is a leap year when it divides by 4, **except** years that divide by 100, which are not, **unless** they also divide by 400.
starter: // Decide, then print "Leap year" or "Common year"
hints: `year % 4 == 0` is true when the year divides by 4 with nothing left over.
There are two ways to be a leap year: divides by 4 but not by 100, **or** divides by 400.
`bool leap = (year % 4 == 0 && year % 100 != 0) || year % 400 == 0;` then choose the text with a ternary or an `if`/`else`.
